description: I’m a student at Veritas University with hands-on experience building Ground Station projects, and I’m looking for driven teammates to build winning, innovative hackathon solutions.
summary: GAIA lets anyone choose an area on Earth and learn, from NASA-ISRO NISAR radar data, what has changed on the ground, starting with flooding and surface water. Radar sees through clouds and works at night, which matters most during rainy-season floods, when optical satellites are blind. GAIA finds every NISAR Level-2 GCOV acquisition over the chosen area, streams only that small area out of each ~6 GB file, and compares dates to map new and receded water. What sets GAIA apart is honesty about uncertainty: every result reports coverage gaps, product maturity, radar mode and track, flags passes likely affected by heavy recent rain or wind-roughened water, and lists known limitations instead of presenting a map as certain. We built and tested GAIA on Lagos, Nigeria, a coastal megacity with recurring floods, and found 20 NISAR acquisitions on two orbit tracks between June and October 2026. GAIA is built to grow into vegetation, ground-deformation and urban-change engines.
details:
What it does. GAIA is a backend pipeline and API that turns raw NISAR radar observations into answers about surface change for any user-chosen area. Version 1 focuses on water: where flooding appeared or receded between two dates.

How it works. Four layers:

  1. Discovery. Uses ASF’s asf_search to find every NISAR L2 GCOV acquisition over the area and time range. It reports track, orbit direction, radar mode, polarization, product maturity and how much of the area each pass covers, and it detects coverage gaps, including NISAR’s documented 27 Jul–10 Aug 2026 gap. For Lagos it found 20 acquisitions (HH+HV, 40 MHz) on track 15 (ascending) and track 152 (descending), every 12 days from June to October 2026.
  2. Ingestion. Uses openSEPPO to stream only the pixels inside the area from each ~6 GB HDF5 file and save them as small Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs, so no full downloads are needed.
  3. Processing. Classifies water in each date from HH/HV backscatter, then compares dates on the same orbit track to produce a change map (unchanged / new water / receded water).
  4. API. A FastAPI service returns the change map together with a full uncertainty report.
